_note: JSE conformance corpus — DATA-SHAPING GRAMMAR (2026-08-12). Computed object keys, nested destructuring with defaults and rest, destructured arrow params, and `localeCompare`. Every case here was measured FAILING before the wave that added it, and two of them failed SILENTLY WRONG rather than loudly: `{ [k]: 1 }` evaluated to `{ k: <value of k> }`, and `([a, b]) => a + b` bound the whole pair to one name and returned a stringified row. Those two had no clean workaround and no error, which is why they were the ones worth adding grammar for — the remainder of the JS data surface (map/filter/reduce/sort/spread/Object.*/JSON/regex/template literals) already passed. Scope: Swift = reference, Kotlin :core runs these via ConformanceTest, TS via conformance.test.ts.

cases.name: computed-key-alongside-plain-keys
cases.expression:
[0].map(z => { const o = { a: 1, [k]: 2 }
return o.a + o.b })[0]

cases.name: computed-key-groups-rows
cases._note: Expressed with array methods rather than a `for` body: the EXPRESSION tier (JSE.evalBlock) is a bounded block with no loop statements by design, and this corpus runs there as well as in the action runner. What it pins is the computed key, not the iteration.

return b })[0]

return c })[0]

cases.name: destructure-default-sees-earlier-binding
cases.expression:

return b })[0]

cases.name: destructure-object-rest
cases.expression:
[0].map(z => { const { a, ...rest } = { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }
return rest.b + rest.c })[0]

cases.name: destructure-nested-from-element
cases.expression:
[0].map(z => { const rows = [{ p: { q: 4 } }]
const { p: { q } } = rows[0]
return q })[0]
cases._note: The iteration binding itself is covered by `param-nested-destructure`; this pins the same pattern in a DECLARATION, which is the shape the expression tier can run.
